lessons.title: Science measures the world
lessons.story: Professor Newton points to a signal tower on the Academy wall. If every traveler reported light with a different number system, nobody could compare experiments or trust measurements across towns.
lessons.summary: Scientists use standard constants and units so experiments can be compared anywhere in the world.
lessons.intuition: A constant is a value we treat as fixed in a given situation. The speed of light in vacuum is one of the most important constants because it sets the scale for how fast information and light can move.
lessons.workedExample: If light travels at 3 x 10^8 meters each second, then in 2 seconds it covers about 6 x 10^8 meters. The number is huge, which is why light seems instant in everyday life.
lessons.mistake: Do not confuse 10^8 with 10^6. That would make light one hundred times slower than it really is.
lessons.takeaway: Shared constants let scientists in different places compare results and build on each other's work.

question.q: What is the speed of light in a vacuum?
question.hint: It is about 300 million meters per second.
question.explain: The speed of light in a vacuum is about 3 x 10^8 meters per second.

lessons.title: Chemistry uses symbols as shorthand
lessons.story: In the Academy kitchen, two flasks look identical until the labels are read. One is water, and one is hydrogen peroxide. A tiny symbol difference changes the substance completely.
lessons.summary: Chemical formulas tell you which atoms are present and how many of each are bonded together.
lessons.intuition: A chemical formula is like a compact recipe. It tells you what atoms are present and how many of each belong in one molecule.
lessons.workedExample: H2O means one water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. If the formula were H2O2 instead, that would be hydrogen peroxide, which behaves very differently.
lessons.mistake: Do not read H2O as H + 2O. The subscript belongs only to hydrogen in this formula.
lessons.takeaway: Small changes in a formula can represent an entirely different substance.

question.q: What is the chemical formula for water?
question.hint: Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
question.explain: Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom.

lessons.title: Units help engineers communicate
lessons.story: An Academy apprentice reports a machine using '12 power' instead of giving the unit. The engineer cannot tell whether that means current, voltage, or power until the unit is named correctly.
lessons.summary: Each physical quantity has a standard unit so people do not confuse current, force, energy, or power.
lessons.intuition: Numbers alone are not enough. Units tell you what kind of quantity you are measuring and keep people from mixing unlike things.
lessons.workedExample: A wire carrying 2 A and a battery supplying 12 V are not interchangeable facts. One tells you charge flow; the other tells you electrical push.
lessons.mistake: Do not mix ampere, volt, watt, and ohm. They describe different electrical ideas.
lessons.takeaway: A correct number with the wrong unit can still lead to a wrong design decision.

question.q: Which unit measures electrical current?
question.hint: It is named after Andre-Marie Ampere.
question.explain: The ampere is the SI unit for electrical current.

lessons.title: Scientific notation handles extreme numbers
lessons.story: The Academy librarian needs to record both the mass of a proton and the distance to a distant star on the same page. Writing out all those zeros would fill the whole page — so the notation compresses them.
lessons.summary: Scientific notation writes any number as a value between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10.

definitions.meaning: the coefficient, a number between 1 and 10
the exponent, shows how many places the decimal moves

lessons.intuition: Positive exponents mean the number is large. Negative exponents mean the number is tiny. The exponent just counts how far the decimal point moved.
lessons.workedExample: 0.0045 becomes 4.5 x 10^-3. The decimal moved 3 places to the right, so the exponent is negative 3. Similarly, 6500 becomes 6.5 x 10^3.
lessons.mistake: Do not confuse positive and negative exponents. 10^-3 means one thousandth, not negative one thousand.
lessons.takeaway: Scientific notation makes it easy to compare and compute with numbers across many orders of magnitude.

question.q: Which correctly expresses 4500 in scientific notation?
question.hint: Move the decimal until one digit is left of it, count the moves.
question.explain: 4500 = 4.5 x 10^3. The decimal moved 3 places left, giving exponent 3.

lessons.title: Vectors have direction, scalars do not
lessons.story: Two runners at the Academy both travel at 5 m/s. One goes north, the other goes east. They have the same speed but different velocities, because velocity carries direction.
lessons.summary: A scalar is a single number with units. A vector is a quantity with both magnitude and direction.

definitions.meaning: magnitude only, like speed or temperature
magnitude and direction, like velocity or force

lessons.intuition: Speed says how fast. Velocity says how fast and which way. The direction part matters when forces cancel, paths cross, or components need to be combined.
lessons.workedExample: A car going 60 mph north and a car going 60 mph east both have the same speed, but their velocity vectors point differently. They would collide at an intersection if timed poorly.
lessons.mistake: Do not treat velocity as just a bigger word for speed. The direction distinction matters in every force and momentum calculation.
lessons.takeaway: Vectors require both a number and a direction. Forgetting the direction makes the answer incomplete.

question.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
question.hint: Which one needs both a number and a direction to be fully described?
question.explain: Velocity is a vector. It requires both magnitude (speed) and direction. Temperature, mass, and speed are scalars.

lessons.title: Acceleration changes velocity
lessons.story: A training cart in Physics Keep starts from rest on a straight track. Each second, its speed increases by the same amount, so the knights can predict its future motion.
lessons.summary: If an object starts from rest and accelerates steadily, its velocity grows linearly with time.
lessons.intuition: Acceleration tells you how quickly velocity changes. If acceleration stays constant, each extra second adds the same speed change.
lessons.workedExample: If u = 0 m/s, a = 5 m/s^2, and t = 3 s, then v = 0 + 5 x 3 = 15 m/s. Starting from rest makes the calculation simpler because the first term is zero.
lessons.mistake: Do not confuse velocity with acceleration. Velocity is how fast you are going; acceleration is how fast velocity changes.
lessons.takeaway: Constant acceleration creates a straight-line growth pattern in velocity over time.

question.q: An object starts from rest and accelerates at 5 m/s^2. What is its velocity after 3 seconds?
question.hint: Start with u = 0 and use v = u + at.

lessons.title: Force and acceleration are linked
lessons.story: A gate in Physics Keep is blocked by a heavy crate. Two students push with the same force, but the lighter practice crate speeds up much more than the heavy one.
lessons.summary: Newton's second law says acceleration increases with force and decreases with mass.
lessons.intuition: Force is the push or pull. Mass is the object's resistance to changing its motion. More push increases acceleration, but more mass makes the same push less effective.
lessons.workedExample: If F = 30 N and m = 10 kg, then a = F / m = 30 / 10 = 3 m/s^2. Dividing by mass tells you how much acceleration each kilogram gets from the push.
lessons.mistake: Do not leave the formula as F = ma when solving for acceleration. Rearrange it first to a = F / m.
lessons.takeaway: A light object and a heavy object do not respond the same way to the same force.

question.q: A 10 kg object has a net force of 30 N. What is its acceleration?
question.hint: Rearrange the formula to a = F / m.

lessons.title: Motion stores energy
lessons.story: A steel ball rolling down the Keep's ramp is easy to stop at low speed, but much harder to stop once it is moving fast. That extra difficulty is stored energy.
lessons.summary: Moving objects carry kinetic energy, and that energy increases with the square of speed.
lessons.intuition: Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed, but speed matters even more because it is squared. Doubling speed multiplies the speed term by four.
lessons.workedExample: If m = 2 kg and v = 4 m/s, then KE = 1/2 x 2 x 4^2 = 16 J. The square happens before the multiplication by mass.
lessons.mistake: Do not forget to square the speed. Using 4 instead of 4^2 would cut the energy way down.
lessons.takeaway: Fast-moving objects become much more energetic very quickly.

question.q: What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg object moving at 4 m/s?
question.hint: Square the speed first.

lessons.title: Gravity pulls objects down at a steady rate
lessons.story: A trainee in Physics Keep drops a stone off the tower wall. No matter how heavy the stone is, it gains the same speed each second on the way down. The ground does not care about mass.
lessons.summary: Near Earth's surface, gravity accelerates every object downward at about 9.8 m/s^2, regardless of mass.

definitions.meaning: about 10 m/s faster downward each second

lessons.intuition: Galileo showed that a feather and a bowling ball dropped in a vacuum hit the ground at the same time. Mass does not change how fast gravity pulls — it only affects the total force, not the acceleration.
lessons.workedExample: After 1 second of freefall from rest, an object reaches 9.8 m/s. After 2 seconds, 19.6 m/s. The speed added each second is the same constant 9.8.
lessons.mistake: Do not confuse weight (F = mg) with mass. A heavier object has more weight but falls at the same acceleration.
lessons.takeaway: In freefall, all objects accelerate equally regardless of mass. Gravity is an equal-opportunity puller.

question.q: An object is dropped from rest. What is its speed after 2 seconds? (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
question.hint: Use v = g x t with u = 0.

lessons.title: Work transfers energy through force
lessons.story: A knight pushes a supply cart across the courtyard of Physics Keep. The longer the distance and the harder the push, the more energy she transfers to that cart.
lessons.summary: Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance. Power is the rate of doing that work.
lessons.formula: W = F d  |  P = W / t

definitions.meaning: distance moved in direction of force

lessons.intuition: Pushing hard over a long distance does a lot of work. Doing that same work quickly requires a lot of power. A slow lift and a fast lift can do the same work; the fast one just needs more power.
lessons.workedExample: If F = 50 N and d = 4 m, then W = 50 x 4 = 200 J. If that work is done in 2 seconds, P = 200 / 2 = 100 W.
lessons.mistake: Work requires motion in the direction of the force. Holding a heavy box still does zero work, no matter how tired your arms get.
lessons.takeaway: Work and power are related but different. Work is total energy transferred. Power is how fast that transfer happens.

question.q: A 50 N force moves an object 4 m. How much work is done?
question.hint: W = F x d

lessons.title: Elements are defined by protons
lessons.story: Dr. Curie holds up carbon and oxygen samples. They look different because their atoms have different numbers of protons in the nucleus, which changes the identity of the element itself.
lessons.summary: An element's atomic number tells you how many protons are in its nucleus.

definitions.meaning: positively charged particles in the nucleus

lessons.intuition: If you change the proton count, you change the element. Six protons means carbon. Eight protons means oxygen. The proton count is the element's identity tag.
lessons.workedExample: Carbon has 6 protons, so its atomic number is 6. If an atom had 7 protons instead, it would not be carbon anymore; it would be nitrogen.
lessons.mistake: Do not confuse atomic number with mass number. Atomic number counts protons only.
lessons.takeaway: Protons decide what the element is, not how heavy the atom happens to be.

question.q: What is the atomic number of carbon?
question.hint: Carbon has six protons.
question.explain: Carbon's atomic number is 6 because it has 6 protons.

lessons.title: Atoms bond in different ways
lessons.story: In the Alchemy Lab, one sample dissolves into charged ions while another stays together as shared electron pairs. The kind of bond explains the difference.
lessons.summary: Covalent bonds share electrons, while ionic bonds transfer them.
lessons.intuition: Bonds are about what atoms do with electrons. Sharing creates covalent bonds. Taking and giving creates ionic bonds.
lessons.workedExample: In a water molecule, atoms share electrons, so the bonding is covalent. In table salt, sodium gives up an electron and chlorine takes it, so the bonding is ionic.
lessons.mistake: Do not assume every solid uses the same kind of bond. Different materials are held together in different ways.
lessons.takeaway: Looking at electron behavior helps you predict the kind of bond.

question.q: Which type of bond involves sharing electrons?
question.hint: Think of atoms holding electrons together.
question.explain: Covalent bonds form when atoms share electron pairs.

lessons.title: Chemists count in moles
lessons.story: The lab ledger cannot list every atom in a sample one by one, so chemists use a giant counting unit called the mole to talk about manageable amounts of matter.
lessons.summary: A mole is a counting unit for atoms and molecules, just like a dozen is a counting unit for eggs.
lessons.intuition: A mole does not describe mass by itself. It describes how many particles you have. It is chemistry's version of a giant bundle count.
lessons.workedExample: If you have 1 mole of water molecules, you have 6.022 x 10^23 molecules. That is far too many to count one at a time, so the mole makes the number usable.
lessons.mistake: Do not confuse a mole with a gram. One is a particle count; the other is a mass unit.
lessons.takeaway: The mole lets chemists talk about enormous numbers of particles in a practical way.

question.q: How many particles are in one mole?
question.hint: This is Avogadro's number.

lessons.title: The pH scale measures acidity
lessons.story: Dr. Curie sets out three vials along the lab bench: lemon juice, pure water, and baking soda solution. Each one has a different number on the pH meter, and that number predicts how it reacts with other materials.
lessons.summary: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, and above 7 is basic.

definitions.meaning: concentration of hydrogen ions in solution

lessons.intuition: A lower pH means more hydrogen ions and a more acidic solution. Each step on the scale is a factor of 10, so pH 3 has 10 times more hydrogen ions than pH 4.
lessons.workedExample: Lemon juice has a pH near 2. Water has pH 7. Bleach has pH near 12. Moving from pH 7 to pH 5 means the concentration of hydrogen ions increased by 100 times.
lessons.mistake: Do not think pH 0 is the strongest possible acid in all situations. Concentrated sulfuric acid can go below pH 0.
lessons.takeaway: pH is a compact way to describe acidity. Each unit change represents a tenfold difference in ion concentration.

question.q: Which pH value represents a basic (alkaline) solution?
question.hint: Basic solutions have pH above 7.
question.explain: pH 10 is above 7, so it is basic. pH 7 is neutral. Below 7 is acidic.

lessons.title: Matter exists in different states
lessons.story: A flask of water in the Alchemy Lab can be ice, liquid, or steam depending on the temperature. The same molecule, H2O, behaves completely differently in each state because of how much energy the particles carry.
lessons.summary: The state of matter depends on how much kinetic energy the particles have compared to the forces holding them together.

definitions.meaning: particles flow but stay in contact
particles move freely and spread out

lessons.intuition: Adding energy (heat) gives particles enough motion to break free from their neighbors. Removing energy makes them slow down and pack together. The state is just a description of how loosely or tightly packed the particles are.
lessons.workedExample: Ice melts at 0 C because water molecules gain enough energy to start sliding past each other. At 100 C, they gain enough energy to escape the liquid surface and become steam.
lessons.mistake: Do not confuse temperature with heat energy. A large cold object can hold more total energy than a small hot one.
lessons.takeaway: States of matter are not fixed properties of a substance. They change with energy and pressure.

question.q: In which state do particles have the most freedom of movement?
question.hint: Think about which state has no fixed shape or volume.
question.explain: Gas particles move freely and fill any container. Solids keep their shape; liquids take the container shape but keep their volume.

lessons.title: Derivatives measure change
lessons.story: At the Math Citadel, a scout tracks how fast the mountain road rises. The important question is not just the height, but how quickly the height changes from one step to the next.
lessons.summary: The derivative tells you how quickly one quantity changes as another changes.

definitions.meaning: take the derivative with respect to x

lessons.intuition: A derivative answers the question 'how fast is this changing right now?' The power rule is one of the fastest ways to compute that change for simple powers of x.
lessons.workedExample: For x^3, the power rule says bring the exponent down and subtract one from the exponent. That turns x^3 into 3x^2.
lessons.mistake: Do not keep the power at 3 after differentiating. The exponent drops by one.
lessons.takeaway: Derivatives turn a function into a new function that describes its rate of change.

question.q: What is the derivative of x^3?
question.hint: Bring the exponent down and subtract one from the power.

lessons.title: Linear equations encode rate
lessons.story: A messenger in the Citadel earns the same extra pay for every mile traveled. That steady rate shows up as the slope in a linear equation.
lessons.summary: In y = mx + b, the slope m tells you how much y changes when x increases by one.
lessons.intuition: Linear equations combine a starting value with a constant rate. If x goes up by 1 each time, y goes up by m each time.
lessons.workedExample: In y = 3x + 5, the slope is 3. That means each time x increases by 1, y increases by 3. The +5 is just the starting offset.
lessons.mistake: Do not confuse the slope m with the intercept b. The intercept tells you where the line starts, not how steep it is.
lessons.takeaway: The coefficient of x in slope-intercept form is the rate.

question.q: What is the slope of y = 3x + 5?
question.hint: The slope is the coefficient of x.
question.explain: In y = 3x + 5, the slope m is 3.

lessons.title: Geometry turns shape into measurement
lessons.story: A circular courtyard in the Citadel must be tiled. To estimate materials, the builders need area, not just the boundary length.
lessons.summary: Area formulas let you compare how much space different shapes cover.
lessons.intuition: Circle area depends on the radius squared, so making the radius just a little larger grows the covered space quickly.
lessons.workedExample: If r = 2, then A = pi x 2^2 = 4pi. Square the radius first, then multiply by pi.
lessons.mistake: Do not use 2r inside the square unless the formula asks for diameter. This formula uses radius.
lessons.takeaway: The radius controls the area strongly because it is squared.

question.q: What is the area of a circle with radius 2?
question.hint: Square the radius before multiplying by pi.

lessons.title: The Pythagorean theorem links sides of right triangles
lessons.story: A scout at the Citadel wants to know the straight-line distance across a rectangular field without walking the diagonal. She walks 3 km east and 4 km north instead, then calculates.
lessons.summary: In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the two shorter sides.

definitions.meaning: the two shorter sides (legs) of the right triangle
the hypotenuse, the side opposite the right angle

lessons.intuition: The hypotenuse is always longer than either leg, but shorter than their sum. The relationship is exact for right angles and approximate for others.
lessons.workedExample: If a = 3 and b = 4, then c^2 = 9 + 16 = 25, so c = 5. The 3-4-5 triangle is the most famous example and appears often in engineering and architecture.
lessons.mistake: Do not add the sides directly. a + b does not equal c. You must square, add, then take the square root.
lessons.takeaway: Pythagorean triples like 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 are worth memorizing. They come up in distance, force, and vector problems.

question.q: A right triangle has legs of length 3 and 4. What is the hypotenuse?
question.hint: Apply a^2 + b^2 = c^2 and solve for c.

lessons.title: Quadratic equations describe curved relationships
lessons.story: A cannonball launched from the Citadel wall follows a parabolic path. The height at each second is not a straight line — it curves down because gravity accelerates the ball.
lessons.summary: A quadratic equation has an x^2 term and can model parabolic motion, area problems, and optimization.

definitions.meaning: two solutions: one with + and one with -
b^2 - 4ac, tells you how many real solutions exist

lessons.intuition: Quadratics often have two solutions because a parabola can cross the x-axis at two points. The discriminant tells you if there are 2 real solutions (positive), 1 (zero), or none (negative).
lessons.workedExample: For x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0, a=1, b=-5, c=6. Discriminant = 25 - 24 = 1. Solutions: (5 ± 1) / 2 = 3 or 2. Both values check out: (3-2)(3-3)=0 and (2-2)=0.
lessons.mistake: Do not forget the ± sign. There can be two valid answers, and both matter in physical or geometric contexts.
lessons.takeaway: The quadratic formula always works for any quadratic, even when factoring is not obvious.

question.q: How many real solutions does x^2 + 4x + 5 = 0 have? (discriminant = 16 - 20 = -4)
question.hint: A negative discriminant means no real square root.
question.explain: Discriminant = b^2 - 4ac = 16 - 20 = -4. Negative means no real solutions.

lessons.title: Circuits connect voltage, current, and resistance
lessons.story: Circuit Golem points to a dim lamp in Engineers Haven. The battery is fine, but the path through the circuit resists charge flow. To predict what happens, engineers use Ohm's law.
lessons.summary: Ohm's law is one of the first tools engineers use to predict electrical behavior.

definitions.meaning: resistance, how strongly the circuit opposes flow

lessons.intuition: Voltage pushes charge through a circuit. Resistance fights that motion. Current is the actual flow you get after those two effects interact.
lessons.workedExample: If I = 2 A and R = 5 ohms, then V = I x R = 2 x 5 = 10 V. That means a 10-volt push is needed to drive 2 amps through 5 ohms of resistance.
lessons.mistake: Do not memorize only one arrangement. If you need current instead, rearrange to I = V / R.
lessons.takeaway: Voltage, current, and resistance are linked. If one changes, at least one of the others must respond.

question.q: If current is 2 A and resistance is 5 ohms, what is the voltage?
question.hint: Multiply current by resistance.
question.explain: V = I x R = 2 x 5 = 10 V.

lessons.title: Distributed loads add up
lessons.story: A bridge deck in Engineers Haven carries a steady line of weight across its length. Before checking stresses, the engineers first convert that spread-out load into a total load.
lessons.summary: Engineers often convert load per unit length into total load before analyzing structures.
lessons.formula: total load = load per length x length

definitions.meaning: combined force from the whole span

lessons.intuition: A distributed load is like repeating the same force amount over and over along a beam. To get the total force, multiply the repeated amount by how far it extends.
lessons.workedExample: If the load is 10 N/m across 4 m, then total load = 10 x 4 = 40 N. The 'per meter' and the meters cancel, leaving newtons.
lessons.mistake: Do not add the load per meter directly to the length. They are different quantities and must be multiplied.
lessons.takeaway: Total load comes from both intensity and span length.

question.q: What is the total load of 10 N/m over 4 m?
question.hint: Multiply the distributed load by the full length.

lessons.title: Efficiency compares useful output to input
lessons.story: An engine in Engineers Haven turns fuel into motion, heat, and noise. Only part of the input becomes useful work, so engineers measure how much value the system keeps.
lessons.summary: No real machine is perfectly efficient, so engineers compare useful energy out to total energy in.
lessons.intuition: Efficiency is a comparison, not a raw amount. It tells you what fraction of what you put in becomes useful output.
lessons.workedExample: If a machine gives 80 J of useful output from 100 J of input, then efficiency = 80 / 100 x 100% = 80%.
lessons.mistake: Do not let efficiency exceed 100% in a normal machine. That would imply you got more useful energy out than total energy in.
lessons.takeaway: Good engineering reduces wasted energy, but real systems always lose something.

question.q: A machine gives 80 J of useful output from 100 J of input. What is its efficiency?
question.hint: Divide useful output by total input, then convert to percent.

lessons.title: Stress tells you how hard a material is working
lessons.story: A pillar in Engineers Haven supports a heavy roof. Two pillars of the same material but different cross-sections carry the same load differently — the thinner one works much harder and may fail first.
lessons.summary: Stress is the internal force per unit area inside a material. High stress means the material is being stretched or compressed intensely.
lessons.intuition: The same force spread over a larger area creates less stress. That is why snowshoes distribute your weight over snow — the stress per unit area drops below what the snow can hold.
lessons.workedExample: If F = 1000 N is applied to a rod with A = 0.01 m^2, then stress = 1000 / 0.01 = 100000 Pa = 100 kPa. Doubling the area halves the stress.
lessons.mistake: Do not confuse force and stress. A thin wire under 10 N can break where a thick cable under 1000 N is fine, depending on area.
lessons.takeaway: Material failure depends on stress, not total force. Area matters as much as load.

question.q: A force of 500 N acts on a cross-section of 0.05 m^2. What is the stress?
question.hint: sigma = F / A

lessons.title: Resistors in series and parallel behave differently
lessons.story: An apprentice in Engineers Haven wires two light bulbs. One circuit makes both bulbs dim when one is unscrewed. The other circuit leaves one bright. The wiring pattern is the difference.
lessons.summary: Series resistors add directly. Parallel resistors reduce total resistance because current has more paths.

definitions.meaning: components connected end-to-end, same current through each
components connected side-by-side, same voltage across each

lessons.intuition: In series, resistance stacks up. In parallel, current finds multiple routes, so total resistance goes down. Adding a parallel path always lowers overall resistance.
lessons.workedExample: Two 10-ohm resistors in series give 20 ohms. The same two in parallel: 1/R = 1/10 + 1/10 = 0.2, so R = 5 ohms. Half the resistance, double the current at the same voltage.
lessons.mistake: Do not add resistors in parallel the same way as series. Parallel resistors always give a result smaller than the smallest individual resistor.
lessons.takeaway: Circuit topology — how parts are connected — changes behavior as much as the component values do.

question.q: Two 6-ohm resistors are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
question.hint: In series, resistances simply add.
